items.title: Funded Through December 11: Inside the Senate Deal That Pushed a Shutdown Fight Past the Midterms
items.body:
## A Last-Minute Deal Averts a October 1 Shutdown

With the federal government's fiscal year set to end on September 30, Senate leaders from both parties reached a bipartisan agreement on a continuing resolution (CR) that keeps federal agencies funded through **December 11**. The deal cleared the chamber with support from members on both sides of the aisle, narrowly avoiding a lapse in funding that would have forced a shutdown of non-essential government operations just as the new fiscal year began.

Continuing resolutions are a routine, if imperfect, tool Congress uses when lawmakers cannot finish the full appropriations process on time. Rather than passing all twelve annual spending bills individually, a CR extends current funding levels for a set period, giving negotiators more time to hash out the details of a longer-term budget without interrupting government services, paychecks for federal workers, or benefit payments that millions of Americans rely on.

## Why December 11 Matters

The choice of a December deadline is notable for what it avoids as much as what it accomplishes. By setting the next funding cliff for after Election Day in November, the agreement effectively removes government funding as an active flashpoint during the final stretch of the midterm campaign season. Lawmakers on both sides have historically been wary of high-stakes shutdown fights coinciding with elections, since the political fallout from a shutdown can be unpredictable and tends to affect incumbents of both parties.

That said, pushing the deadline to December doesn't resolve the underlying disagreements that have made full-year appropriations difficult to pass in recent years. Disputes over the size of discretionary spending, funding priorities for specific agencies, and policy provisions attached to spending bills remain unsettled. Congressional leaders on both sides have described the extension as a way to "buy time" rather than a resolution, meaning a similar negotiation — potentially with higher stakes — is likely to resurface in the weeks after the midterm elections.

## What a Continuing Resolution Does and Doesn't Do

For everyday Americans, a CR generally means government operations continue largely as before: federal employees keep working, agencies keep running, and services like Social Security, veterans' benefits, and mail delivery continue uninterrupted. However, CRs typically freeze spending at prior-year levels and can limit agencies' ability to start new programs or initiatives, which is why lawmakers and agency officials often view them as an imperfect stopgap rather than a substitute for regular budgeting.

Markets and federal contractors also tend to watch these deadlines closely, since even short shutdowns can disrupt payments, delay contract awards, and create uncertainty for businesses that rely on federal funding cycles.

## The Road Ahead

With the immediate shutdown threat postponed, attention now shifts to what happens after the midterms. Analysts note that "lame duck" sessions of Congress — the period after an election but before newly elected members are sworn in — have historically been used to tackle major, unfinished legislative business, including large spending packages. Whether this December deadline results in a full set of appropriations bills, another short-term extension, or a renewed standoff will likely depend on the outcome of the midterm elections and how the balance of power in Congress shifts as a result.

For now, the bipartisan agreement represents a temporary truce in Washington's recurring budget battles — one that keeps the government open while leaving the harder questions for lawmakers to settle later this year.

items.title: From 35% to 60%: How Warsh's Hawkish Jackson Hole Speech Flipped Wall Street's Rate Bets Overnight
items.body:
## A Jackson Hole Surprise Nobody Priced In

Heading into last week's Jackson Hole Economic Symposium, most traders had a simple story in their heads: inflation was cooling, the labor market was softening, and the Federal Reserve was on a glide path toward cutting interest rates at its September meeting. Futures markets reportedly had the odds of a rate hike at roughly 35%, with many desks treating that figure as a formality more than a real risk.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh tore that script up.

In his keynote address at the symposium, Warsh struck a notably hawkish tone, describing recent inflation readings as "concerning" and telling the audience of central bankers, economists, and investors that the Fed "will have work to do" before it can declare victory over price pressures. The remarks were widely interpreted as a signal that the central bank is far less comfortable with the current inflation trajectory than markets had assumed — and possibly open to tightening policy further rather than easing it.

## Rate Bets Flip in a Matter of Hours

The market reaction was swift. According to trading desks tracking interest-rate futures, the implied probability of a September rate hike jumped from around 35% to roughly 60% in the hours following the speech — a dramatic repricing for a market that, just a week earlier, had been leaning toward cuts.

Equities moved in the opposite direction. Major U.S. stock indexes slipped as investors digested the prospect of tighter-for-longer monetary policy, with rate-sensitive sectors such as technology and real estate said to be among the hardest hit. Short-dated Treasury yields, which move closely with rate expectations, climbed as bond traders scrambled to adjust their positioning.

Analysts described the move as one of the more abrupt sentiment shifts of the year, noting that it underscores how quickly market narratives can unravel when a single speech contradicts the prevailing consensus.

## Why Warsh's Words Carry Extra Weight

Because the Fed chair's public remarks are scrutinized for clues about the future path of monetary policy, even carefully hedged language can move markets. Investors and economists parse word choice, tone, and emphasis for signs of where the committee's thinking is heading — and Warsh's use of terms like "concerning" landed as a clear departure from the more measured, data-dependent language markets had grown used to.

Some strategists cautioned against overreacting to a single speech, pointing out that the Fed's actual September decision will still hinge on incoming inflation and employment data released in the weeks ahead. Others argued that Warsh's tone reflects a genuine shift in the committee's internal debate, with more officials reportedly growing wary that inflation progress has stalled.

## What Investors Are Watching Next

With rate-hike odds now nearly split with expectations for a hold, attention turns to the next batch of economic reports — particularly consumer price and jobs data — which could either reinforce or unwind the market's new hawkish lean. Traders are also expected to parse comments from other Fed officials in the coming days for signs of whether Warsh's view reflects broader consensus on the committee or a more personal emphasis.

For everyday investors, the episode is a reminder of how sensitive markets remain to Fed communication, and how quickly rate expectations — and portfolio values — can shift on a single speech. As always, market-implied probabilities are estimates based on trading activity, not guarantees of the Fed's eventual decision, and conditions can change quickly as new data arrives.
